title: Hosted API demo - Chat & text generation basics (Halcyon Retail)
summary: Intro demo of Redwood Hosted API focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, core parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop), retry behavior and idempotency, and quick tour of Console and Optimize recommendations. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a conversational shopping assistant; security and data residency are top concerns.
next_steps: Jordan Lee - send tailored pricing and a 30-day pilot plan by 2026-04-01
Samir Gupta - share example benchmark script and suggested prompt sets by 2026-03-30
Erica to confirm stakeholders and timeline for pilot by 2026-04-03
action_items: Samir Gupta: benchmark script + prompt set examples (due 2026-03-30)
Marcus Yang: provide current infra diagram and token volumes (due 2026-03-30)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-27 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~47m | Attendees: Jordan Lee, Samir Gupta (Redwood) — Erica Stone, Marcus Yang, Lena Park (Halcyon)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I think we have about 45 minutes, I'll give a quick intro then Samir will do a live demo of the hosted API for chat and text generation. Erica, Marcus, thanks for taking the time, do you want to do a 30s intro?

[00:18] Erica Stone: Yeah thanks, I'm Erica, Head of ML at Halcyon Retail. We're building a shopping assistant that helps customers with product discovery and returns, integrations with order system. Key thing for us is latency — we need snappy responses on web and mobile — and data residency, we have EU customers and some regs.

[00:34] Marcus Yang: Marcus here, platform eng, we run K8s in GCP, currently hitting OpenAI for prototype but exploring hosted alternatives for control and cost predictability. We do about 2M requests / month currently during peak.

[00:50] Jordan Lee: Awesome, that's helpful. Goal for today's demo is show basic chat flows, streaming (which gives the user-perceived latency improvement), how to tune params, and what happens with retries. Samir, over to you.

[01:05] Samir Gupta: Cool thanks. I'll share my screen — give me a sec. (screen share) Alright, this is the Redwood Console — quick note, the API surface is the same whether hosted or dedicated, so the SDK calls you'll write will be portable.

[01:28] Samir Gupta: Starting with a chat example — you can call /v1/chat/completions, include messages array, model param. For streaming set stream=true and we will send incrementally as tokens are generated. That reduces perceived latency because client can render tokens asap rather than waiting for full completion.

[01:50] Lena Park: Are there client SDKs that handle reconnects for streaming?

[01:55] Samir Gupta: Yes we have SDKs (JS, Python) that support streaming and handle resumable reconnect logic in many cases; but important: streaming over websockets vs SSE vs chunked HTTP, depending on your infra. We also recommend idempotency keys for non-streaming or to dedupe retries.

[02:15] Samir Gupta: Quick demo: simple chat prompt, temperature 0.2 for deterministic suggestions, max_tokens 150, top_p left default. I'll show how changing temperature to 0.8 increases variability.

[02:31] (typing, demo)

[02:40] Samir Gupta: Here's a sample response with stream enabled — you'll see events every ~200ms with partial tokens. The Console also renders the streamed output. In our experience streaming reduces time-to-first-token by 30-60% depending on model and sequence length.

[03:02] Erica Stone: For web UX, time-to-first-token is huge. Do you have recommended chunk sizes or buffer strategy?

[03:10] Samir Gupta: We recommend render as you get tokens and use a debounce of ~50-100 ms to avoid janky UI. For mobile, smaller chunks are better. Also watch network MTU and proxies; long-lived connections can be interrupted so have a reconnect strategy.

[03:30] Marcus Yang: How do retries work with streaming enabled? If the connection drops mid-token do we re-request and get duplicate content?

[03:38] Samir Gupta: Great question. If a streaming connection drops, the client should re-request using the same idempotency key; for streamed responses we provide resume tokens in some cases, but generally we recommend making final responses idempotent or using short checkpoints. For critical flows we suggest a non-streamed fallback with the same input hash to dedupe. Also Redwood SDK will by default retry transient errors with exponential backoff and will not automatically retry non-idempotent ops unless you opt in.

[04:10] Jordan Lee: Important to call out: retries are safe for GET-style stateless prompts if you include an idempotency key; for multi-step stateful chat you should store conversation state server-side and rehydrate on retry.

[04:28] Samir Gupta: Moving on to params — big ones are temperature, max_tokens, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, and stop sequences. Use temperature 0-0.3 for deterministic completions (e.g., product attributes), up to 0.8 for creative suggestions. max_tokens controls output length — we meter tokens both input and output.

[04:58] Lena Park: How do you recommend handling safety / hallucination for product claims? We can't have the model invent specs.

[05:06] Samir Gupta: Two levers: prompt engineering and post-filtering. For critical fields, use structured outputs with JSON schema or function calling so model returns constrained fields. Redwood Console supports strong schema validation and function/tool calling to reduce hallucination. Also set temperature low and provide grounding context (product catalog snippets).

[05:36] Marcus Yang: You mentioned function calling — is that the same as tools? Any SDK examples?

[05:42] Samir Gupta: Yes, function calling (we call them tools) lets you declare shapes and Redwood will try to fill them; we have examples in the SDK repo. It's supported in streaming as well. I'll share links after the call.

[06:00] Samir Gupta: Next, rate limits and retries — our hosted API has tiered rate limits; for spikes we recommend client-side exponential backoff with jitter, and consider batch endpoints for embeddings or rerank jobs. For chat we do continuous batching on the server side to improve throughput without hurting latency.

[06:28] Erica Stone: Any advice for cost control? We're sensitive to token price.

[06:34] Samir Gupta: Yes: 1) lower max_tokens where possible; 2) prefix caching for repeated prompts, Redwood supports automatic prefix/KV cache; 3) use smaller model variants for less-critical tasks; 4) use sampling params to reduce expected output size; 5) use Redwood Optimize suggestions — it will recommend quantization and batching settings per workload.

[06:58] Jordan Lee: To add, Redwood Optimize can run an eval suite on your prompt set and recommend model/quantization combos to hit a latency/cost target. It gives per-route token cost breakdown in Console.

[07:12] Marcus Yang: Is quantization available on hosted or only for Dedicated/private?

[07:18] Samir Gupta: We have quantized variants available in hosted catalog for many open models — for the most aggressive quantization sometimes Dedicated gives more control, but hosted offers vetted quantized builds with performance profiles.

[07:32] Lena Park: Can we route EU customers to EU hardware to satisfy residency?

[07:36] Jordan Lee: Yes — smart routing can pin by region; we have EU regions and can set policy to prefer EU-hosted instances. For strict residency we also offer Private deployment (VPC) where data never leaves your network.

[07:52] Erica Stone: On security — do you have SOC 2, encryption at rest, KMS?

[07:58] Jordan Lee: Yes SOC 2 Type II, AES-256 at rest, TLS in transit, and we integrate with customer KMS / HSM for Dedicated and Private. We also provide audit logs and RBAC. I'll share our security pack link.

[08:14] Marcus Yang: Regarding logs — we need logs for debugging but don't want PII stored. Can logs be redacted?

[08:20] Samir Gupta: We support configurable logging retention and redaction rules; for hosted, you can opt into not persisting inputs, or have them stored only for X days. For regulated data we recommend Private deployment plus your KMS.

[08:38] Jordan Lee: Quick architecture note — typical flow for us: client -> Redwood edge -> model serving runtime (GPU pool) -> optional cache layer -> return. If you're routing by region we can configure that policy.

[08:55] Samir Gupta: Back to demo — I'll show code snippet in Python using our SDK: create client, call chat.create with messages and stream=True, handle events. (demo code scroll)

[09:20] Samir Gupta: Example: 
client.chat.create(model='redwood-chat-1', messages=[...], temperature=0.2, stream=True, idempotency_key='halcyon-12345')

[09:34] Samir Gupta: For retries the SDK exposes retry config; we default to 3 attempts for 5xx with backoff, but not for 4xx. You can also disable automatic retries and implement your own logic if you need fine-grained control.

[09:50] Marcus Yang: Do you provide metrics for token usage per request? We need to bill internal teams.

[09:56] Jordan Lee: Yes Console has token-level breakdown per request and per-route. You can export to S3 or pull via API for internal billing.

[10:10] Lena Park: Any SLA for hosted?

[10:14] Jordan Lee: Hosted has best-effort uptime; for guaranteed SLAs we recommend Dedicated which has monthly commit and SLA-backed latency/uptime. Hosted is often fine for early pilots.

[10:26] Erica Stone: For pilot we probably start with hosted, then move to Dedicated if we need predictability. Timeline: 30-60 days to validate.

[10:36] Samir Gupta: Sounds reasonable. I'll also run a small benchmark showing latency p50/p95 and cost per 1k tokens using your sample prompts. Can you share a representative prompt set?

[10:45] Marcus Yang: We'll share CSV of 50 prompts and expected output shapes plus average user sessions per day.

[10:52] Samir Gupta: Perfect. A few more quick notes — stop sequences: use them when generating structured text; they're evaluated token-wise. If you need exact JSON output, pair with function calling or schema enforcement.

[11:05] Sample transcript continuation: (longer demo) Samir toggles temperature, shows streaming partials, triggers a transient error and demonstrates the SDK's retry logs. There's some cross-talk.

[16:40] Speaker 4: Sorry, got a quick question on caching — how long does prefix caching hold?

[16:45] Samir Gupta: Depends on TTL you set; default is short (minutes) for dynamic user prompts, but you can configure up to days for stable prompts. Cache is per-route and keyed by prefix hash. Note: cached tokens still count towards billing in some configs, but Optimize can show net savings.

[17:12] Jordan Lee: The Optimize module will also surface prompts that are high cost and low value so you can prioritize optimization.

[18:01] Erica Stone: Any gotchas with streaming on mobile networks?

[18:06] Samir Gupta: Mobile networks can cause jitter; use smaller heartbeats, be tolerant to partial tokens, and implement UI fallback to spinner if connection lost mid-stream. For very flaky networks, non-streamed responses might feel more stable.

[20:00] Demo wraps up; Samir shows console route metrics and Optimize suggestions for batching and a recommended smaller model for taxonomy extraction tasks.

[20:22] Jordan Lee: Recap — streaming reduces time-to-first-token, use idempotency keys to protect against duplicate results, tune temperature/max_tokens/top_p for quality vs cost, use prefix caching and smaller models for cost control, and we can route by region or move to Private for strict residency.

[20:45] Erica Stone: This was helpful. Next steps: we'll send the prompt set and infra diagram; Jordan you send pilot plan and pricing; Samir shares benchmark script.

[21:00] Jordan Lee: Yep, we'll put everything in a short email after this call and share links to the security pack, SDK repo, and sample scripts. Any final questions?

[21:12] Marcus Yang: One last — do you support SAML SSO for Console?

[21:17] Jordan Lee: Yes SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. We'll include the integration doc.

[21:25] (closing)

Notes / artifacts shared: link to Redwood hosted-api quickstart (https://redwood.ai/quickstart), security pack (internal link), SDK repo (github.com/redwood-inference/sdk), sample benchmark script (attached by Samir).

End of transcript.
